introduction_markdown:
**General Certificate of Education Board - General Certificate of Education Examination. Philosophy 2 (0790), Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), ADVANCED LEVEL, June 2024. Duration: three hours.**

Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section.

Each essay question shall be marked according to the following criteria:
- Coherence and organization of material;
- Clear presentation of the problematic;
- Identification and development of the Thesis, Antithesis, Synthesis and Conclusion as prescribed.

Each question carries 25 marks.

You are reminded of the necessity for good English and orderly presentation in your answers.
incertitudes: Règle de choix : la page de garde dit « Candidates are required to answer FOUR questions, choosing at least one question from each section » (quatre questions au total, au moins une par section ; trois sections de deux questions : Section One 1-2, Section Two 3-4, Section Three 5-6). `regles_choix` porte le minimum, une règle `parmi 1 sur 2` par section ; la règle « 4 questions en tout » n'est pas exprimable en entier et est recopiée dans `introduction_markdown`.

Points : chaque question est imprimee « 25 marks » (4 x 25 = 100). Les questions de textes (5 et 6) ont leurs points par sous-question : Q5 = 5 + (2 x 2) + 3 + 4 + 4 + 5 = 25 ; Q6 = 5 + (2 x 2) + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 25. Aucun écart de somme constaté, aucun point corrigé. La page de garde de 2024 ne donne pas de barème par partie pour les dissertations (contrairement à 2022) : les titres « (5 marks) », « (7 marks) »... des corrigés de dissertation ne sont donc pas utilisés, seule la structure exigée (problématique, thèse, antithèse, synthèse, conclusion) est suivie.

Aucun corrigé officiel : les corrigés sont des réponses modèles rédigées de mémoire, sans accès à une source. Les auteurs et positions cités sont ceux de l'histoire de la philosophie établie, sans citation littérale, sans numéro de page et sans date ; à faire relire par un enseignant de philosophie avant mise en avant.

Sujet scanné (3 pages) avec filigrane gcerevision.com / Kawlo sans incidence sur la lecture ; aucune figure. Page de garde vérifiée : ADVANCED LEVEL, Philosophy 2, Paper 2 (Philosophical Writing and Analysis), code 0790, JUNE 2024, trois heures.

Q2 : le sujet dit « True knowledge starts from reason alone. Examine the validity of this Cartesian assertion. ». Le corrigé expose Descartes (doute méthodique, cogito, idées innées, cire, critère de clarté et distinction), puis Locke, Hume, Arnauld (cercle cartésien) et Kant, sans citation littérale hormis les formules classiques « I think, therefore I am » et « thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind » (paraphrase de Kant). Descartes n'affirme pas lui-même que l'expérience est inutile en physique : le corrigé le dit.

questions.enonce_markdown:
True knowledge starts from reason alone. Examine the validity of this Cartesian assertion.

(25 marks)
questions.corrige_markdown:
**Introduction and problematic.** For René Descartes (seventeenth century), philosophy needs a foundation as certain as mathematics. In the *Discourse on Method* and the *Meditations* he proposes to reject everything that can be doubted and to rebuild knowledge on a first indubitable truth, reached by the mind alone. The assertion to be examined is that true knowledge starts from reason alone, without any help from the senses. The problem: can reason alone, without sense experience, produce true and certain knowledge, or does it need experience as its starting point? The question is that of the *origin* and the *validity* of knowledge, the old quarrel between rationalism and empiricism.

**Thesis: Descartes' claim and its justification.**
- *Methodical doubt.* The senses sometimes deceive us (a tower that looks round from afar is square), we cannot be sure that we are not dreaming, and an "evil demon" could deceive us even in mathematics. Whatever depends on the senses is therefore uncertain.
- *The cogito.* Even if I doubt everything, I cannot doubt that I doubt, hence that I think: "I think, therefore I am". This first truth is discovered by the mind in itself, not given by experience. It is clear and distinct, and becomes the criterion of truth: whatever I conceive as clearly and distinctly is true.
- *Innate ideas.* In the Third Meditation, Descartes distinguishes innate ideas (those of God, of the self, of extension and of mathematical truths), adventitious ideas (coming from the senses) and factitious ideas (made by the mind). The idea of the infinite God cannot come from a finite being like me; it is placed in my mind by God, which is the "trademark" argument. These ideas, held by the understanding, are the foundation of the rest.
- *The wax example.* In the Second Meditation, a piece of wax changes in all its sensible qualities when it is melted, and yet we judge it to be the same wax. What we know of it is not given by the senses or the imagination but by the understanding alone (intellectual inspection). Even bodies are known by reason.
- *The model of mathematics.* Certain knowledge (geometry, arithmetic) is obtained by deduction from simple and evident intuitions, without the help of experience.

**Antithesis: the claim is open to serious objections.**
- *Locke* rejected innate ideas: the mind at birth is a blank slate (*tabula rasa*) and all our ideas come from experience, by sensation and reflection. Children and people from other cultures do not show the "innate" ideas Descartes assumes. *Hume* went further: all ideas are copies of impressions; relations of ideas (mathematics) are certain but tell us nothing about the world, while matters of fact rest on experience and habit, not on reason alone.
- *Circularity.* Arnauld pointed out the "Cartesian circle": Descartes proves God's existence by clear and distinct ideas, and then uses God's goodness to guarantee that clear and distinct ideas are true. The foundation is therefore not secure.
- *The solitary reason has no content.* From "I think, therefore I am", it is hard to deduce the existence of the external world without relying on the very faculties (senses, imagination, memory) that were doubted. Descartes himself admits in his scientific writings that experiments are necessary to decide among the many possible explanations of nature.
- *Modern science and psychology* show that knowledge of nature progresses by observation and experiment, and that the development of reasoning itself depends on experience, language and society.

**Synthesis.** *Kant* proposed a way beyond the dispute: "thoughts without content are empty, intuitions without concepts are blind". Knowledge begins with experience, but it does not all arise from experience: reason supplies the forms (space, time, categories) by which experience is ordered. Thus Descartes is right that reason has an active, structuring role and that certainty in mathematics and logic does not come from the senses; but he is wrong to claim that it can start and succeed alone. Descartes' claim is valid for the *order of certainty* in mathematics and for the first truth of the cogito; it is not valid for knowledge of the empirical world.

**Conclusion.** The Cartesian assertion is only partly valid. It stands for the role of reason in the foundation of certainty and for the criticism of the unreliable senses, but it fails as a complete theory of knowledge because of the difficulties of innate ideas and the circle, and because empirical knowledge requires experience. A balanced view recognises that both reason and experience are needed.
